passage:
The target board in the back room of the phone shop in Leeds had Nadia's name in red: 14 contracts out of 30, nine days left. Her rent was due on the first.
When Noa walked in asking about a cheaper plan, Nadia smiled wide and asked about Noa's weekend, the dog in the lock-screen photo, the cracked case. She meant the warmth. She also knew it worked.
"Honestly, I'd grab this deal now. These go fast," she heard herself say. The deal ran till the end of the month. It did not go fast.
Noa laughed, then said, "Can you print me the full terms? I'll compare at home."
Something in Nadia loosened. "Of course," she said, and printed them, including the line about the price rise in year two. After Noa left, she stood looking at the board for a while.

qa.q: How many contracts had Nadia sold, out of how many?
qa.a: Nadia had 14 contracts out of 30, with nine days left.

qa.q: What did Nadia feel when Noa asked for the printed terms?
qa.a: Nadia felt relief, as if the pressure she had been putting on was released; "something in Nadia loosened" and she printed everything honestly.

qa.q: What did Noa's approach get right?
qa.a: Noa enjoyed the friendly chat but judged the offer by the written terms, not by the warmth or the "these go fast" line.

qa.q: How might Nadia's day look different without the red name on the board?
qa.a: Without the target and the rent worry, Nadia might not have felt the need to say "these go fast" at all, and her warmth would carry less pressure.

grounding: A salesperson under a monthly target and rent pressure uses warmth and a false hurry, while the buyer checks the written terms instead.

passage:
At the front desk of FitZone Community Gym, the sales team's monthly chart hung beside the water dispenser. Rafiq was two memberships short of his bonus, and his younger sister's college fees were due.
Still, when a nervous woman in office clothes asked about joining, he walked her round the machines, told her the evening crowd was heavy, and offered the free one-week trial. He really believed the gym could help her; he had lost his own back pain there.
From the next desk he could hear Jomon: "Only two annual slots left at this price, sir, after today it's full." There were forty slots. Rafiq had seen the list.
Later, by the lockers, Jomon said, "You're too soft. Trial people never come back."
Rafiq thought about his chart. "Some do," he said. The woman in office clothes signed up after her trial week.

qa.q: What did Rafiq offer the woman in office clothes?
qa.a: Rafiq offered her the free one-week trial.

qa.q: Why was Rafiq tempted to push harder, and what held him back?
qa.a: He felt pressure from being two memberships short of his bonus and his sister's fees, but he believed the gym could truly help, so he stayed honest.

qa.q: How could a buyer at this desk tell the two sellers apart?
qa.a: By their behaviour, not their friendliness: a buyer could ask to see the slot list and prefer the seller who offers a trial over the one who says "after today it's full".

qa.q: What would change for Jomon's customers if they asked to see the list?
qa.a: They would find forty slots instead of two, see that the urgency was invented, and could decide at their own pace.

grounding: Two gym salespeople under the same targets act differently: one believes in the product and stays honest, the other bends the truth with false urgency.

passage:
Floor supervisor's note, appliance store, 29th
Month-end. Yash is four units short of target and it shows: he has been at the entrance since opening, smiling at everyone, calling customers "sir" and "aunty" within a minute.
At 3 pm I heard him tell a couple that the washing machine they liked was "the last piece, price goes up tomorrow". We have eleven in the back and no price change planned. His voice stayed cheerful, but he wouldn't look at me afterwards.
Avni, at the next counter, told a customer honestly that the cheaper model would suit a two-person home better. She lost the bigger commission on that sale and didn't seem to mind.
What I did next: I spoke to Yash privately, said the "last piece" line has to stop, and said I know the targets are heavy. We agreed he'll correct it with the couple if they come back. I have also raised the target pressure with the regional manager.

qa.q: How many units short of target was Yash?
qa.a: Yash is four units short of target.

qa.q: What does Yash avoiding the supervisor's eyes suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Yash felt guilty or uneasy about the 'last piece' line, even though his voice stayed cheerful.

qa.q: What protective step could the couple take when told 'last piece, price goes up tomorrow'?
qa.a: They could pause, ask to see the stock or come back the next day, judging the claim itself rather than the friendly smile.

qa.q: How might Avni's customer see her advice?
qa.a: Avni recommended the cheaper model that suited a two-person home, so her customer is likely to trust her even though she earned less.

grounding: Shows a salesperson under month-end targets using warmth and a false 'last piece' line, beside a colleague who sells honestly.

passage:
Friday, 10 pm
Closed three site visits today. Ujjwal rang the little bell for me in front of the whole team. I should feel great.
The first two were fine. I believe in these flats; the light in the east rooms is lovely, and I said so because it's true.
The third family, though. The father kept asking about the loan and the mother kept looking at the kids. I heard myself say, "Only two left on this floor, and prices go up Monday." Only the first half is true. Nobody told me anything about Monday. It just came out, in my friendliest voice, because my incentive depends on the 30th.
They booked. The little girl hugged me.
Now I can't stop thinking about the Monday line. Tomorrow I'll call and tell them there's no confirmed price change, so they can take their time.
Lakshmi

qa.q: What did Lakshmi tell the third family?
qa.a: 'Only two left on this floor, and prices go up Monday.'

qa.q: What is Lakshmi feeling that night, despite the bell?
qa.a: Lakshmi feels guilty and uneasy; the Monday line was not true, and Lakshmi can't stop thinking about it even after being celebrated.

qa.q: What is Lakshmi's plan to set things right, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Calling tomorrow to say there is no confirmed price change, so the family can decide at their own pace instead of under a false deadline.

qa.q: How might the third family feel if they found out later that the Monday rise was made up?
qa.a: They would likely feel misled and start doubting even the true parts of Lakshmi's warmth, which is why correcting it quickly matters.

grounding: Shows a salesperson under an incentive deadline who believes in the product yet slips in a false urgency line, and decides to correct it.

passage:
Rukmini: 2 memberships short and it's the 28th
Joseph: same. manager wants the "founder rate ends tonight" line on every call
Rukmini: it ended last month too. and the month before
Joseph: I know. I just say it fast
Rukmini: had a guy today who really wanted to get stronger for his knees. I liked him. told him about the trainer who does the gentle classes. that part I meant
Rukmini: then I said "tonight only" and he looked panicked and signed
Joseph: commission is commission 🤷
Rukmini: is it though. I felt sick after
Joseph: ...yeah. me too sometimes
Rukmini: tomorrow I'm calling him to say the rate isn't really ending. he can take a few days and decide
Joseph: ok. maybe I'll drop the line too. scared of the target though

qa.q: What line does the manager want on every call?
qa.a: The manager wants the 'founder rate ends tonight' line on every call.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel after the customer signed?
qa.a: Rukmini felt sick and guilty, because the 'tonight only' line made a customer Rukmini genuinely liked panic into signing.

qa.q: What could a buyer learn from this chat?
qa.a: A seller's friendliness can be real while the deadline is not, so a buyer can ask whether the rate truly ends and take a few days before signing.

qa.q: What is it like for Joseph when Rukmini decides to drop the line?
qa.a: Joseph feels pulled both ways: uneasy about the line too, yet scared of missing the target if he stops using it.

grounding: Shows gym salespeople under monthly targets using a false deadline alongside genuine warmth, and one deciding to stop.

passage: By four o'clock Lavanya had knocked on nineteen doors in Karimganj and sold nothing. Her target for the month was twelve water purifiers; she had four. Arnab, her area manager, had texted twice: "Push harder. Say the offer ends today." At the twentieth house, an elderly couple invited her in for tea. Lavanya smiled her brightest smile, called the woman Mashi, admired her garden. The words came out smoothly: "Only today, this price. Tomorrow it goes up." It wasn't true; the price had been the same for months. The old man reached for his wallet. Lavanya felt her cheeks go hot. She did believe in the purifier; her own family used one. But the lie sat heavy in her throat. "Actually, Mesho," she said, "the price will be the same next week too. Talk to your son first." They didn't buy that day. Walking back to the bus stand, she wondered what she would tell Arnab.

qa.q: How many purifiers had Lavanya sold against her target of twelve?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel after saying the offer ended today?
qa.a: Lavanya felt ashamed, her cheeks hot and the lie heavy in her throat, even though she believed in the purifier.

qa.q: What would you advise buyers dealing with a very friendly seller?
qa.a: Judge what the seller does, not the warmth: check whether a today-only claim is true, and take time to talk to family before buying.

qa.q: How might the elderly couple see Lavanya's correction?
qa.a: They may feel respected and trust her more, since she told them the truth even though it cost her a sale.

grounding: Shows a salesperson under targets using urgency and warmth, who believes in the product but catches herself bending the truth.
